title: All-Butter Pie Crust
dek: Cold butter, cold water, and the discipline to stop mixing while it still looks wrong.
yield: Two 9 inch crusts, enough for one double-crust pie
intro:
All-butter crust tastes better than anything else and it is the least forgiving of the fats, because butter is about fifteen percent water and it melts at a temperature your hands comfortably exceed. Everything below is aimed at keeping distinct sheets of solid butter inside the dough right up until they hit the oven, where the water in them flashes to steam and pushes the layers apart.

The dough should look shaggy and underhydrated when you stop working it. If it looks like a smooth ball, you have gone too far, and the crust will come out of the oven tough rather than flaky. Cold and undermixed beats warm and tidy every time.

items: 255 g unsalted butter, very cold, in 1/2 inch cubes
6 tbsp ice water, plus up to 2 tbsp more
1 large egg beaten with 1 tbsp cream, for the wash

method: Cube the butter and put it back in the freezer for 15 minutes. Mix the ice water and vinegar and keep them in the fridge. The vinegar slightly inhibits gluten and makes the dough more forgiving of handling.
Whisk flour, sugar and salt in a wide bowl. Add the butter and toss it so every cube is coated.
Flatten each cube between your thumb and forefinger into a rough sheet, working quickly. You want flat shards, not peas and not crumbs. Those sheets become the layers.

Sprinkle in the ice water and vinegar a tablespoon at a time, tossing with a fork after each. Stop as soon as the mixture holds together when you squeeze a handful, even though the bowl still looks like rubble.

Tip it onto the counter and push the pile away from you a few times with the heel of your hand, folding it back over itself. Six or seven pushes, no more. This is what makes the layers long rather than random.
Divide, press into two flat discs rather than balls, wrap and refrigerate at least an hour. A disc chills evenly and rolls out without cracking; a ball does neither.

Roll on a lightly floured counter from the centre outward, turning the disc a quarter turn after every few passes so it does not stick and stays round. If the butter starts to smear or the dough goes slack, stop and put it back in the fridge for ten minutes.
Ease the dough into the pan rather than stretching it. Stretched dough shrinks back in the oven and you get a crust that has slumped halfway down the sides.
Chill the shaped shell for at least 30 minutes before baking, and freeze it if you have time. Cold dough into a hot oven is the whole game.

Bake in a hot oven, generally 400 to 425°F (205 to 220°C) to start, until the crust is set and pale gold at the edges before you drop the temperature. If you are checking a filled pie for doneness, an instant-read thermometer pushed into the centre of the filling should read close to 200°F (93°C), which is where fruit starches finish thickening.

What goes wrong: warm butter. If your kitchen is above about 70 degrees Fahrenheit (21°C), work faster, chill between every step, and consider running the food processor for the first stage rather than your hands.
notes: Weigh the flour. A cup of flour can vary by thirty grams depending on how it was scooped, and that is the difference between a supple dough and a dry one.
The dough freezes for three months as discs. Thaw overnight in the fridge, never on the counter.
storage: Wrapped discs keep three days in the fridge. A rolled and fitted shell keeps two days covered in the fridge and freezes well in the pan, wrapped twice.

title: Lard Crust
dek: The old crust, and still the flakiest one, provided you get the right lard.
intro:
Lard makes a flakier crust than butter and it is not close. Lard is nearly pure fat with almost no water, its crystals are large and soft, and it coats flour more thoroughly, which means less gluten and more shatter. What it does not do is taste like butter, which is why this version uses both and lets each one do its job.

The catch is sourcing. Shelf-stable hydrogenated lard from a supermarket tastes of nothing good. What you want is leaf lard, rendered from the fat around the kidneys, which is neutral and clean. Anything rendered from back fat carries a savoury note that is fine in a chicken pie and strange in a berry one.

items: 115 g leaf lard, cold, in cubes
115 g unsalted butter, cold, in cubes
7 tbsp ice water, plus more as needed
1 large egg beaten with 1 tbsp milk, for brushing

method: Chill the lard and butter until they are genuinely hard. Lard softens at a lower temperature than butter and it goes from workable to greasy without much warning.

Whisk the flour, salt and sugar. Cut the lard in first, rubbing it in until the mixture looks like coarse sand throughout. Lard coats flour more completely than butter does, and this stage is where the tenderness comes from.

Add the butter and flatten the cubes between your fingers into sheets, leaving them visible. Those sheets are where the flakes come from. The two fats are doing two different jobs, which is why they go in at different times.
Add the ice water and vinegar a tablespoon at a time, tossing with a fork, and stop the moment a squeezed handful holds. The dough will look drier than a butter dough and that is correct.
Gather, divide, flatten into two discs, wrap and chill an hour.
Roll from the centre out, turning as you go. Lard dough rolls more easily than butter dough and tears less, which is one of the reasons people who grew up on it never switched.
Fit it into the pan without stretching, trim, crimp, and chill the shell for 30 minutes before it goes near heat.

Bake at 400 to 425°F (205 to 220°C) until the crust is a deep even gold, the base is dry and firm when you lift the pie and look underneath, and the edges have browned properly. Lard browns a shade faster than butter, so start checking earlier than you would otherwise.
For a filled fruit pie, look for filling bubbling thickly in the centre and not just at the rim, or check with an instant-read thermometer for a filling temperature near 200°F (93°C).

What goes wrong: the wrong lard. Hydrogenated block lard from a shelf makes a crust that is technically flaky and tastes faintly of a chip shop. Ask a butcher for leaf lard, or render your own from leaf fat over low heat until the cracklings are golden and the fat runs clear.
notes: Half lard, half butter is the version most people prefer. All lard is flakier and tastes plainer; all butter tastes better and is less flaky. Pick your compromise.
Rendered leaf lard keeps six months in the fridge and a year in the freezer, and it is worth rendering a batch when a butcher has leaf fat.
storage: Discs keep three days refrigerated, three months frozen. A baked empty shell keeps two days at room temperature under a cloth.

title: Blind Baking, Properly
dek: The fix for a soggy bottom, and the reason your custard pie had a raw seam.
intro:
Blind baking is baking a crust before, or entirely without, its filling. You do it whenever the filling will not be in the oven long enough to cook the pastry underneath it, which covers every cream pie, every custard, and any fruit pie with a very wet filling.

The two problems it solves are slumping walls and a raw base. The two problems it creates, if done carelessly, are a crust that shrinks down the sides and a base that puffs into a dome. Weight and cold dough solve both, and there is a specific order of operations that matters more than any single trick.

items: 1 batch pie dough, one disc, chilled
2 lb (900 g) pie weights, dried beans or rice
1 large sheet of parchment or heavy foil

method: Roll the dough a good two inches wider than the pan so there is enough to come up the sides and over the rim without stretching. Stretched dough is dough that will shrink.
Ease it into the pan and press it firmly into the corner where the base meets the wall. Air trapped in that corner is exactly where a shell collapses.
Trim, leaving an overhang, then fold it under and crimp. Leaving the rim slightly thicker gives you insurance against shrinkage.
Freeze the shell solid, at least 30 minutes and ideally an hour. This matters more than the weights. Frozen fat does not start moving until the structure of the crust has already set.
Line the frozen shell with parchment, pushing it right into the corner, and fill it to the very top with weights. Half-filling the shell leaves the upper walls unsupported and they will slump inward.
Bake at 400°F (205°C) until the edges are set and beginning to colour and the surface under the parchment looks dry and matte rather than damp. Lift a corner to check.

Remove the parchment and weights and return the shell to the oven. Bake until the base is dry, firm and a light gold, with no translucent patches left. This is the step people cut short, and it is why the bottom is pale.
For a fully baked shell, keep going to a deep even gold. For a partially baked shell that will go back in with a filling, stop at pale gold.
Brush the hot base with beaten egg white and return it for two minutes so it sets into a thin waterproof seal. This is the single best defence against a wet filling soaking in, and it costs nothing.
If the base has puffed anyway, press it flat with the back of a spoon while it is still hot and soft. It will stay where you put it.

For a custard filling going into this shell, remember it is an egg product with its own doneness point. Bake a custard until the edges are set and the centre wobbles as one mass rather than rippling, which lands around an internal temperature of 175 to 180°F (79 to 82°C). Past that and it curdles and weeps.
notes: Rice and dried beans work as weights forever, and they can go back in the jar and be reused indefinitely. They will no longer cook, so keep them labelled for the purpose.
A second pie pan nested inside the shell also works, though it browns the walls less evenly than loose weights do.
storage: A baked shell keeps two days at room temperature loosely covered, and freezes for a month baked. Do not refrigerate a baked shell uncovered; it goes soft from the humidity.

title: A Lattice Top
dek: Twenty minutes of weaving, and the vents are the functional part.
intro:
A lattice is not only decoration. A wet berry pie under a solid lid traps steam, the filling boils rather than reduces, and the top crust steams from below into something pale and damp. A lattice lets water leave, which concentrates the filling and browns the strips from both sides.

The weaving is easier than it looks and impossible if the dough is warm. Everything here is a rhythm of roll, chill, weave, chill, and the chilling is not padding.

items: 1 large egg beaten with 1 tbsp cream
1 ruler or a straight-edged pastry cutter
1 rimmed baking sheet lined with parchment
2 sheets of parchment for chilling the strips

method: Roll the dough into a rectangle a little larger than the pie, about an eighth of an inch thick. Slide it, on parchment, onto a sheet pan and refrigerate 15 minutes until firm.
Cut strips with a ruler and a sharp knife or a fluted wheel. Anywhere from half an inch to an inch wide, but pick one width and stay with it; uneven strips look accidental rather than rustic.
Chill the cut strips again on the tray. Warm strips stretch as you lift them and end up thin and torn.
Lay every second strip across the filled pie in one direction, evenly spaced, and leave the alternates aside.
Fold back every other strip halfway. Lay one strip across the pie perpendicular to them, then unfold the folded strips back over it.

Now fold back the strips that were underneath, lay the next perpendicular strip, and unfold. Repeat outward from the middle in both directions. That alternating fold is the entire technique, and once your hands do it once they remember.

Trim the ends to about half an inch beyond the pan, then fold the bottom crust overhang up over them and crimp the whole rim together. That seal is what keeps the filling from escaping under the strips.
Chill the assembled pie in the freezer for 20 minutes. This is the step that separates a crisp defined lattice from one that spreads and merges into a lid.
Brush with egg wash, avoiding puddles in the gaps, and scatter coarse sugar over.

Bake starting hot, around 425°F (220°C), until the lattice is set and beginning to colour, then drop to 375°F (190°C) and continue until the strips are a deep golden brown and the filling is bubbling thickly through the gaps in the centre of the pie, not just around the rim.
If you want a number, an instant-read thermometer in the middle of the filling should be near 200°F (93°C), which is where fruit starch has finished doing its work.
What goes wrong: weaving on a warm counter in a warm kitchen. If the strips start feeling greasy and stretchy at any point, put the whole tray in the fridge and go do something else for ten minutes.
notes: A woven lattice looks better than strips simply laid over each other, and the difference is about four minutes of work.
For a shortcut, cut wide strips and lay them in a simple over-and-under grid. Nobody has ever complained about a pie because of the weave.
storage: An assembled unbaked lattice pie freezes solid on a tray, then wraps and keeps three months. Bake it from frozen, adding time, and it is arguably better than one baked fresh.

title: Marionberry Pie
dek: The state's best berry, and it releases enough juice to flood a badly built pie.
intro:
The marionberry is a blackberry cross bred at Oregon State and named for the county, and it is darker, more acidic and more aromatic than the blackberries growing over every fence in this valley. It is also very wet, which is the whole engineering problem of a marionberry pie.

Two things make it work. Enough starch for the amount of juice the fruit will actually release, which is more than you think, and a genuinely long cooling period. A pie cut warm is a pie that runs across the plate, and the cooling is when the starch sets, not an afterthought.

items: 6 cups marionberries, fresh or frozen, about 850 g
3/4 cup granulated sugar, more if the fruit is sharp
5 tbsp instant tapioca or 1/3 cup cornstarch
1 batch all-butter pie dough, two discs
1 large egg beaten with 1 tbsp cream

method: If the berries are frozen, do not thaw them. Frozen fruit tossed with starch and baked from frozen gives up its liquid gradually into a filling that is already thickening, where thawed fruit dumps it all at once.
Toss the berries with sugar, starch, lemon juice, zest and salt. Let the bowl sit 15 minutes so the starch hydrates and the sugar starts drawing juice.
Taste a berry with the sugar on it. Marionberries vary enormously; early ones are sharp and late ones are almost sweet enough on their own. Adjust now rather than regretting it later.
Line a 9 inch pan with the bottom crust, letting it overhang, and chill it while you roll the top.
Fill the shell, mounding the fruit slightly in the centre because it will settle, and dot the butter over the top.
Add the top crust or a lattice, seal and crimp the rim firmly, and cut generous vents if you have gone with a solid top. Steam has to leave or the filling boils and the crust steams.
Freeze the assembled pie 20 minutes, then brush with egg wash and scatter coarse sugar.
Bake at 425°F (220°C) on a preheated sheet pan on a low rack for 20 minutes. The hot pan under the pie is what cooks the bottom crust, and it is the difference between crisp and pale.

Drop the oven to 375°F (190°C) and continue until the crust is deep golden brown all over and the filling is bubbling thickly and slowly in the centre, not just around the edge. Thick slow bubbles mean the starch has activated; thin fast ones mean it has not.

An instant-read thermometer in the middle of the filling should read close to 200°F (93°C). Cornstarch and tapioca both need to get to roughly that temperature to set, and a pie pulled at the point where the edges look right is usually short in the centre.
Cool the pie completely on a rack, at least four hours and preferably overnight. This is not optional and it is not conservative advice. Warm fruit pie filling is liquid.
What goes wrong: not enough thickener for very wet fruit, and cutting it early. If your pie ran, one of those two things happened, and it was probably the second.
notes: Rock Creek Preserves marionberry jam sits on the local shelf here for the eleven months a year when the fresh berries are not around. A pie built on jam is a different thing, but a good one.
Frozen marionberries are as good as fresh for pie and often better, because the freezing ruptures cells and gets the juice moving early.
storage: Room temperature under a cloth for two days, then in the fridge for three more. Fruit pie does not like being refrigerated from the start; the crust goes soft.

title: Blackberry Cobbler
dek: For the berries growing over your fence, which are free and endless and slightly aggressive.
intro:
Himalayan blackberry is a noxious weed in this state and a genuinely excellent pie fruit, which is an awkward combination if you own land. Cobbler is what you make when you have picked far more than any pie could hold and your forearms are scratched to pieces.

Biscuit topping rather than batter, dropped in rough spoonfuls, because that gives you crisp browned tops, soft undersides where they meet the fruit, and gaps for steam to escape. A batter poured over the whole surface seals the pan and steams the fruit into soup.
method: Heat the oven to 375°F (190°C) and butter a 9 by 13 inch dish. Set it on a rimmed sheet pan, because cobbler bubbles over and cleaning an oven floor is a poor use of an evening.
Toss the berries with sugar, cornstarch, lemon and salt and spread them in the dish. Let it sit while you make the topping so the starch hydrates.
Whisk the flour, sugar, baking powder, soda and salt. Cut in the cold butter with your fingertips until the largest pieces are the size of a small bean and the rest is coarse and sandy.
Pour in the buttermilk and stir with a fork just until a shaggy dough forms with dry patches still visible. Overmixed biscuit dough goes tough and dense, and this one has nowhere to hide.
Drop the dough over the fruit in rough spoonfuls, leaving real gaps between them. The gaps are functional. They let steam out and let the fruit reduce instead of boil.
Brush the tops with cream and scatter the coarse sugar heavily. Do not brush the fruit.

Bake until the biscuits are deep golden and firm, the fruit is bubbling thickly around the edges and up through the gaps, and a skewer pushed into the middle of the largest biscuit comes out clean with no wet dough on it.
If the tops are browning before the biscuits are cooked through, tent with foil and keep going. An underbaked biscuit bottom sitting in hot fruit turns to paste, and that is the usual failure here.
An instant-read thermometer in the fruit should be near 200°F (93°C), which is where the cornstarch has fully thickened. Below that the filling stays runny even after it cools.
Cool at least 30 minutes before serving. It will still be warm and it will have gone from soup to something that holds its shape in a bowl.
notes: Wild blackberries are seedier and sharper than cultivated ones. Add a little more sugar and expect a more assertive pie.
This is the correct place for vanilla ice cream, and it is not a garnish.
storage: Covered at room temperature two days, or in the fridge four. Reheat portions in a 325°F (165°C) oven until the fruit bubbles again and the biscuit crisps.

title: Apple Pie
dek: Two kinds of apple, a cooked filling, and no gap between the fruit and the lid.
intro:
The classic apple pie failure is the dome: a beautifully browned top crust arched over an inch of empty air, with the fruit collapsed at the bottom. It happens because raw apples are mostly water held in rigid cells, and those cells give way all at once in the oven, after the crust has already set in the shape you built it.

Precooking the filling solves it. The apples release their water on the stove where you can see it, the pieces firm up, and what goes into the shell is very close to what comes out. It also lets you thicken the juice accurately instead of guessing.

items: 3 lb (1.4 kg) apples, half firm tart and half sweet, peeled and sliced 1/4 inch thick
3 tbsp cornstarch mixed with 3 tbsp water
1 batch pie dough, two discs, chilled
1 large egg beaten with 1 tbsp cream

method: Use two kinds of apple. A firm tart one that holds its shape, such as Granny Smith or a Gravenstein, and a softer sweet one that collapses into sauce and fills the gaps. All of one kind gives you either apple gravel or apple sauce.
Melt the butter in a wide pan, add the apples, both sugars, lemon, spices and salt, and cook over medium heat, stirring gently.

Cook until the apples have released a good pool of liquid, softened at the edges, and a slice bends without snapping but still holds together when you lift it. That is roughly 8 to 10 minutes and it is a texture, not a time.
Push the apples to one side, stir the cornstarch slurry into the liquid, and cook until it turns from cloudy to glossy and thickens enough to coat the fruit. Stir in the vanilla off the heat.
Cool the filling completely, spread on a sheet pan to speed it up. Warm filling melts the bottom crust before it ever reaches the oven, and this is the most common reason for a soggy base.
Line the pan with the bottom crust and chill it. Fill with the cold apples, packing them in and pressing down so there are no voids, and pour any remaining thickened juice over.
Lay on the top crust, seal, crimp, and cut four generous vents. Freeze the pie 20 minutes, then brush with egg wash and sugar it.
Bake at 425°F (220°C) on a preheated sheet pan on the lowest rack for 20 minutes, then drop to 375°F (190°C).

Continue until the crust is a deep even brown, including the base, which you can check by lifting the pie and looking, and juice is bubbling slowly through the vents. Thick lazy bubbles, not thin fast ones.

An instant-read thermometer in the centre should reach about 200°F (93°C). Because the filling went in precooked, this happens sooner than it would otherwise, and the crust is the limiting factor rather than the fruit.
Cool at least four hours before cutting. The starch is still setting while it cools and a warm slice will slump.
What goes wrong, besides the dome: watery apples like Red Delicious, which turn to mush and give up more liquid than any amount of starch will hold. Buy apples that are meant for baking.
notes: A grating of sharp cheddar into the top crust dough is an old habit in this part of the country and it is very good.
Cooking the filling the day before makes this a much easier project. It keeps three days in the fridge.
storage: Two days at room temperature under a cloth, three more in the fridge. Warm slices briefly in a 325°F (165°C) oven rather than a microwave, which turns the crust to leather.

title: Berry Crisp
dek: Oats, brown sugar, cold butter, and no pastry to worry about at all.
intro:
A crisp is what you make when you want the fruit without the commitment. There is no dough to chill, no lattice to weave, and it works with any berry, any stone fruit and most combinations of the two. The topping is a streusel with oats in it, which is what makes it crisp rather than merely crumbly.

The one place people go wrong is the ratio of topping to fruit. Too thin and it disappears into the juice; too thick and the middle never crisps because it is steaming from below. About three quarters of an inch, rubbled rather than spread, is the right amount.

items: 8 cups mixed berries, about 1.1 kg, fresh or frozen

method: Heat the oven to 375°F (190°C). Butter a 9 by 13 inch dish and set it on a rimmed sheet pan to catch the overflow, because there will be some.
Toss the berries with sugar, cornstarch, lemon and salt and spread them in the dish. If the fruit is frozen, use it frozen and add 10 minutes to the bake.
Combine the flour, oats, brown sugar, nuts, cinnamon and salt in a bowl and add the cold butter.

Rub the butter in with your fingertips until the mixture holds together in clumps when you squeeze a handful, with pieces ranging from crumbs to hazelnut-sized lumps. Uniform crumbs bake into a sandy layer; irregular ones bake into something with texture.
Scatter the topping over the fruit in rubble rather than pressing it into a lid, leaving a few gaps for steam.
Bake until the topping is deep golden and firm to a fingertip, the nuts smell toasted, and the fruit is bubbling thickly up around the edges and through the gaps.

If you want the number, an instant-read thermometer pushed into the fruit should read close to 200°F (93°C), which is where cornstarch finishes thickening. Below that the juices stay thin no matter how brown the top looks.
If the topping browns before the fruit is bubbling, tent it loosely with foil and keep going. Brown topping over cold fruit is the most common way this comes out wrong.
Rest 20 minutes before serving. It sets noticeably as it cools and it is far too hot to eat straight out of the oven anyway.
notes: The topping keeps in a bag in the freezer for three months and goes straight from frozen onto fruit, which makes this a fifteen minute dessert.
Hazelnuts are the local nut and the better choice here. Toast them first if you want the flavour to carry.
storage: Covered at room temperature two days, four in the fridge. Reheat in a hot oven to bring the topping back; a microwave makes it soggy in seconds.

title: Hand Pies
dek: Pie you can eat in a truck, which is the entire design brief.
intro:
A hand pie has one job that a whole pie does not: it has to survive being held. That changes the filling entirely. Anything loose enough to be good on a plate will run out of a hand pie down your wrist, so the filling gets cooked down first until it is more like a thick jam than a pie filling.

The other adjustment is sealing. A hand pie has a long seam relative to its size and every inch of it is a chance to leak. Cold dough, a dry rim, a firm crimp, and a vent in the top so the steam has somewhere to go other than out the side.

items: 4 cups berries, about 550 g, or the same weight of diced apple
3 tbsp cornstarch mixed with 3 tbsp water
1 double batch pie dough, four discs, chilled
1 large egg beaten with 1 tbsp cream

method: Cook the fruit with the sugar, lemon and salt over medium heat until it collapses and releases its juice, then keep going until the volume has dropped by about a third and it smells cooked rather than fresh.

Stir in the cornstarch slurry and cook until the mixture turns glossy and thick enough that a spoon dragged through the pan leaves a track that stays open for a second. Stir in the butter off the heat.
Cool the filling completely, ideally overnight in the fridge. Warm filling melts pastry and a warm hand pie assembled in a hurry will leak.
Roll the dough about an eighth of an inch thick and cut twelve pairs of shapes: rounds about five inches across, or rectangles. Chill the cut shapes on a lined tray for 15 minutes.

Put a heaped tablespoon of filling on the centre of each base, leaving a clear border of at least three quarters of an inch. Overfilling is the leading cause of blowouts and everyone does it the first time.
Brush the border with water or egg wash, lay the top on, and press the air out from the filling toward the edge before you seal. Trapped air expands and splits the seam.
Crimp the edge firmly with a fork, pressing right through both layers, and cut two short vents in the top of each.
Freeze the assembled pies on the tray for 20 minutes. This firms the fat and sets the shape so they do not slump into ovals.

Brush with egg wash and scatter coarse sugar. Bake at 400°F (205°C) until the pastry is deep golden brown all over, the bottoms are firm and browned when you lift one, and any escaping filling has bubbled and caramelised rather than run thin.

Cool on a rack at least 20 minutes. An instant-read thermometer pushed into the filling of one straight from the oven will read near 200°F (93°C), which is to say the filling inside is far hotter than the outside suggests and it has burned more than one impatient person.
If glazing, whisk the powdered sugar, milk and vanilla and drizzle it over the fully cooled pies. Glazing warm pies just makes a transparent sticky film.
What goes wrong: a loose filling. If your first batch leaked, cook the next filling down further. It should mound on a spoon and hold its shape.
notes: Marionberry jam straight from the jar is a legitimate shortcut filling and needs no cooking down at all.
These freeze unbaked and bake from frozen, adding about ten minutes, which makes them the most useful thing in this section.
storage: Two days at room temperature in a tin, five in the fridge, three months frozen. Reheat in a 350°F (175°C) oven for a few minutes to bring the pastry back.

title: Slab Pie
dek: Pie for twenty, in a sheet pan, cut in squares like a sensible person.
intro:
A slab pie is a pie rolled thin in a rimmed sheet pan, and its whole advantage is ratio. Because the layer of fruit is shallow, every square has considerably more crust per bite than a wedge from a deep pie, which is either the best or the worst thing about it depending on which part you like.

It also feeds a crowd from one oven, cuts into neat squares, and travels to a potluck without anybody having to think about a pie server. The shallow filling cooks faster and thickens more reliably, which makes it a more forgiving project than a deep dish pie despite looking like more work.

items: 1 double batch pie dough, made as two large discs
1 large egg beaten with 2 tbsp cream
10 cups berries or sliced fruit, about 1.4 kg
1 tsp ground cinnamon, for apple versions

method: Roll the first disc into a rectangle about eighteen by thirteen inches, which is bigger than it sounds and needs a clear counter. Roll it around the pin to move it, and unroll it over a half sheet pan.
Ease it into the corners without stretching, letting the excess hang over the rim, and chill the lined pan while you make the filling.
Toss the fruit with sugar, cornstarch, lemon and salt. Because the layer is shallow, you need proportionally more starch than a deep pie, which is why the amount looks high.
Spread the fruit in an even layer right to the corners and dot the butter over it. An even layer is what gives you squares that all set to the same firmness.
Roll the second disc to the same size, lay it over, trim to about half an inch beyond the pan, and fold the two edges together and crimp against the rim.
Cut vents generously across the whole top, at least a dozen, or lay a lattice. A large surface area needs a lot of vents.
Freeze the assembled pan 20 minutes, then egg wash and sugar the top.

Bake at 400°F (205°C) until the crust is deep golden brown across the whole surface and the filling is bubbling thickly through the vents in the middle of the pan, not just at the ends. Expect somewhere near 45 minutes and check the middle, which is always last.
An instant-read thermometer in the centre of the filling should read close to 200°F (93°C), which is where the cornstarch has finished setting.
Cool completely in the pan on a rack, at least three hours. A slab pie cut warm slides apart, and the whole point is neat squares.
Glaze if you like, then cut into squares with a bench scraper rather than a knife, pressing straight down.
What goes wrong: an uneven fruit layer. Thin patches burn, thick patches stay loose, and it shows immediately when you cut it.
notes: A quarter sheet pan version halves everything and fits a smaller oven and a smaller gathering.
This is the correct format for a bake sale, a wake, or anything else where somebody needs to feed a room without plates.
storage: Covered at room temperature two days, four in the fridge. It travels better than any other pie in this collection and it is the only one you can stack.

title: Thickeners, Compared
dek: Why your pie leaked, in terms of which starch you used and how much water the fruit had.
yield: One clear idea about how much starch your fruit needs
totalTime: Saves you an afternoon of disappointment
intro:
A pie leaks for exactly one reason: there was more free water in the fruit than the thickener could hold. Everything else, the crust, the oven, the pan, is downstream of that. So the useful skill is not following a number in a recipe, it is looking at the fruit in front of you and deciding how wet it is.

Below are the four thickeners worth knowing, what each one does badly, and rough amounts per quart of fruit. Treat them as starting points and adjust upward for very juicy fruit and downward for anything dense and dry.

ingredients.group: Per quart of prepared fruit, roughly
items: 2 to 3 tbsp cornstarch for medium-wet fruit
3 to 4 tbsp instant tapioca for very wet berries
4 to 5 tbsp all-purpose flour for apples and dense fruit
1.5 to 2 tbsp tapioca starch or arrowroot for a glossy finish
1 tbsp lemon juice, which affects how starches set
1 quart of blackberries or marionberries, the wettest category
1 quart of peaches or cherries, wet but less so
1 quart of apples or pears, comparatively dry
1 quart of frozen fruit, which behaves wetter than the same fruit fresh

method: Cornstarch is the default. It sets firm and clear-ish, it needs to reach roughly 200°F (93°C) to thicken fully, and it thins out again if you boil it hard or too long. It also loses power in the presence of a lot of acid, which matters with rhubarb and sharp berries.

Instant tapioca is the berry specialist. It holds more water than cornstarch, it stays glossy, and it tolerates freezing and reheating without weeping. Its drawback is texture: the granules need at least 15 minutes to hydrate before baking or you get small firm beads in the finished pie.

Flour is the old country answer. It is forgiving, it never breaks, and it produces a cloudy, slightly gluey set that some people find comforting and others find dull. It also mutes the flavour of the fruit more than any other option.

Arrowroot and tapioca starch give the glossiest, cleanest set and the most vivid fruit colour. They are the most expensive, they break down under long baking, and they turn slimy if you use too much. Good for a shallow pie, poor for a deep one.
Judge your fruit before you measure anything. Squeeze a handful. If juice runs freely between your fingers, go to the top of the range. If it barely moistens your palm, go to the bottom.
Understand that frozen fruit is wetter. Ice crystals rupture cell walls, so thawed fruit gives up far more liquid than the same fruit fresh. Bake from frozen, and add roughly a quarter more starch.
Let the mixed filling stand 15 minutes before it goes in the shell, whichever starch you used. Dry starch dropped straight into a hot oven clumps and leaves both watery patches and chalky ones.

Bake until the filling bubbles in the middle of the pie, thickly and slowly, and not just around the rim. Fast thin bubbles at the edge mean the centre has not reached temperature yet and the starch there has not activated.

Cool completely. Every starch on this list continues to set as it cools, and a pie cut at an hour will run even if it was baked perfectly. This is the single most common reason people blame the thickener.

If you have leaked anyway, diagnose honestly. A pie that ran but tasted right was underthickened or undercooled. A pie that was firm but pasty was overthickened. A pie that went watery after a day in the fridge used cornstarch where tapioca would have held.
notes: Never substitute these one for one by volume. Tapioca and cornstarch are roughly comparable, flour has about half the thickening power, and arrowroot has slightly more than cornstarch.
A tablespoon of ground instant tapioca, buzzed in a spice grinder, dissolves invisibly and is the best of both worlds for a berry pie.
storage: Keep starches in sealed jars away from steam. Cornstarch lasts years; instant tapioca goes slowly stale and loses some power after about a year in a humid cupboard.

title: Marionberry Jam
dek: High-acid fruit, so a boiling water bath is the right process, and the times come from a tested source.
totalTime: About 3 hours including the process and cooling
intro:
Marionberries make the best jam of any fruit in this valley, and they are also naturally high in acid, which is what makes them safe to process in a boiling water bath. That is the key distinction in all home preserving. High-acid foods, meaning fruits, jams, jellies and anything pickled with added vinegar, can be safely processed in boiling water. Low-acid foods, meaning plain vegetables, meat, fish and soups, cannot, and need a pressure canner.

This page gives the jam. It deliberately does not print a processing time, because that figure depends on your jar size and your altitude, and printing a number for someone to misapply is worse than sending them to look it up.

items: 1 tbsp butter, optional, to reduce foaming
1 wide heavy-bottomed pot, at least 8 quarts
6 half-pint jars with new lids and sound rings
1 boiling water canner with a rack, or a deep stockpot with a rack
3 small plates in the freezer for testing
1 copy of the current USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning, or your OSU Extension office

method: Get the tested processing time first. Look up the current figure for berry jam in your jar size in the USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning, or call OSU Extension. Time varies by jar size and by altitude, and this recipe will not guess it for you.

Note where you are. Siletz sits close to sea level, so the sea level figures apply here. Water boils cooler as you go up, so anyone canning at elevation adds time according to the tested altitude table. Look up your own altitude rather than assuming somebody else's applies.
Use bottled lemon juice, not fresh. Bottled juice has a standardised acidity; fresh lemons vary, and the acid here is doing a safety job as well as a setting one.
Wash the jars and keep them hot. Bring the canner water up with the rack in it. Have the lids clean and at hand.

Crush the berries in the pot with a potato masher, leaving some texture. Add the sugar and lemon juice and stir over low heat until every grain of sugar has dissolved and the mixture no longer feels gritty on a spoon. Undissolved sugar crystallises in the jar.
Raise the heat and bring it to a full rolling boil, meaning a boil that does not stop when you stir it. Stir constantly and scrape the bottom, because jam scorches the moment you turn away.

Boil hard until it reaches the gel stage. On a thermometer that is 220°F (105°C) at sea level, or roughly 8°C above the boiling point of water where you are. Skim the foam if you did not use the butter.

Confirm with a cold plate. Put a spoonful on a frozen plate, wait 30 seconds, and push it with a fingertip. Set jam wrinkles ahead of your finger and holds a line. Loose jam floods back. Take the pot off the heat while you test or you will overshoot.

Ladle the hot jam into hot jars through a wide funnel, leaving a quarter inch of headspace. Slide a bubble tool around the inside, wipe every rim until it squeaks, and fit lids and rings finger tight.
Lower the jars into the canner on the rack, with water covering them by at least an inch, and process for the tested time you looked up, timed from the moment the water returns to a full boil.
Turn off the heat, wait five minutes, then lift the jars straight up and set them on a towel with space between them. Leave them undisturbed overnight.
Check the seals the next day. A sealed lid is concave and does not flex when pressed. Anything unsealed goes in the fridge and gets eaten within a month, not reprocessed on a whim.

What goes wrong: jam that never sets, which almost always means it never reached the gel stage. It is not a canning safety failure, and you can pour it back into a pot and re-boil it, but you would have to process again in clean jars with new lids.
notes: Nobody at this store has cooked this particular batch. Follow a tested process, and if anything about a jar looks or smells wrong when you open it, dispose of it without tasting.
Local jam is on the shelf here for the eleven months a year when there is no fruit. Rock Creek Preserves does the marionberry one.
storage: Sealed jars keep a year or more in a cool dark cupboard, with the rings removed so a failed seal is visible. Once opened, refrigerate and use within about a month.

title: Blackberry Jam, Seedless or Not
dek: The weed in your fence line, in jars, and the seeds are optional.
intro:
Wild blackberry makes a sharper, more assertive jam than marionberry and it has a lot more seed in it. Whether you strain those seeds out is a matter of household politics; straining costs you about a third of the yield and all of the texture, and produces something closer to a jelly.

Blackberry is high-acid fruit, which is why a boiling water bath is the correct process for it. Low-acid foods such as plain vegetables, meat, fish and soup are not water bath safe under any circumstances and need a pressure canner. That line never moves.

items: 1 food mill fitted with a fine screen, or 1 fine sieve
1 sturdy spoon or ladle for pressing
2 cups extra berries to make up the lost volume
1 boiling water canner with a rack
1 copy of the current USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning, or OSU Extension on the phone

method: Look up the tested processing time for berry jam in your jar size before you start, from the USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning or your Extension office. The figure depends on jar size and altitude and is not printed here on purpose.

Adjust for where you are. Near sea level, which includes Siletz, the base figures apply. Higher up, water boils cooler and the tested altitude table tells you how much time to add. Look up your own elevation.

If going seedless, cook the berries gently with a splash of water until they collapse and the juice runs freely, then pass everything through a food mill or press it through a sieve. Expect to lose roughly a third of the volume to seed and pulp.
Measure what you have after straining and adjust the sugar to roughly three parts fruit to two parts sugar by volume. Adding the full sugar to a reduced quantity of fruit gives you candy.
Combine fruit, sugar and bottled lemon juice in a wide heavy pot over low heat and stir until the sugar is completely dissolved and the mixture feels smooth rather than gritty on the back of a spoon.
Bring it to a full rolling boil that cannot be stirred down, stirring constantly and scraping the bottom corners of the pot where jam catches first.
Boil until it reaches the gel stage, which reads 220°F (105°C) on a thermometer at sea level or about 8°C above whatever the boiling point is where you are.

Test on a frozen plate. A spoonful left for 30 seconds should wrinkle when you push it and hold the track your finger makes. If it floods back, keep boiling and test again in two minutes. Pull the pot off the heat while testing.
Fill hot jars to a quarter inch of headspace, remove bubbles, wipe the rims until they squeak, and fit lids and rings finger tight.

Process in the boiling water canner for the tested time you looked up, with the jars covered by at least an inch of water, timed from the return to a full boil. Rest five minutes off the heat, then lift the jars out onto a towel.
Leave them alone overnight, then check every lid. A sealed lid is dished and rigid. Refrigerate anything that did not seal.

What goes wrong: overcooking. Blackberry jam pushed well past the gel stage turns dark, stiff and slightly bitter, and there is no undoing it. Start testing the moment the thermometer approaches the target.
notes: Half seedless and half whole, combined at the end, gives you jam with body and without the dental experience. It is the version most people actually want.
Never call a home canning recipe safe because it worked once. Follow tested processes, and dispose of any jar that is bulging, spurting or smells wrong without tasting it.
storage: Sealed jars, rings off, a year or more in a cool dark place. Opened jars live in the fridge and are good for about a month.

title: Low-Sugar Jam, and Why It Behaves Differently
dek: Sugar is not only sweetness. Take it out and you have to replace what it was doing.
intro:
Standard jam is roughly equal parts fruit and sugar by weight, and that sugar is doing three jobs. It binds water so microbes cannot use it, it is a structural partner to pectin in forming a gel, and it tastes sweet. Cut it in half and the gel gets weaker, the keeping quality drops, and the jam tastes much more strongly of the fruit, which is the reason people want it.

The replacement is a different pectin. Low-methoxyl pectin sets with calcium rather than with sugar and acid, which is why it works with almost no sugar at all. It is a different product with different instructions, and this is one of the places where following the insert in the box matters more than following any recipe page.

items: 8 cups prepared fruit, about 1.1 kg, crushed
1 to 1.5 cups granulated sugar, or honey, to taste
3 tbsp low-methoxyl pectin, the kind sold for low or no sugar recipes
1 packet calcium powder as supplied with that pectin, mixed per its instructions
1 boiling water canner with a rack
1 copy of the pectin manufacturer's current instructions
1 copy of the USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning, or OSU Extension

method: Start with the tested recipe that came with your pectin. Low-sugar jams are the one category where the manufacturer's insert outranks a general recipe, because the ratios are specific to that product and the safety of the finished jam depends on them.
Then look up the processing time separately in the USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning or with OSU Extension. It varies by jar size and by altitude, and this page prints no number for you to copy.

Remember what changes. Less sugar means less water is bound up, which means a shorter shelf life once opened and a softer set. Fruit is still high acid, so a boiling water bath is still the right process; the sugar is not what made it water bath safe in the first place.
Prepare the calcium water as the packet directs and set it aside. This is the ingredient that actually causes the set in a low-methoxyl pectin, and skipping it gives you fruit sauce.
Crush the fruit in a wide pot, add the lemon juice and the calcium water, and heat until it is steaming and the fruit has slumped.
Mix the pectin powder thoroughly into the sugar before it goes anywhere near the pot. Pectin dropped into hot liquid on its own clumps instantly into rubbery lumps that never dissolve.
Stir the sugar and pectin mixture in and bring it to a full rolling boil that cannot be stirred down. Boil hard for one minute, or for whatever your pectin's instructions say.

Do not judge this by the standard gel stage. A conventional jam is done at 220°F (105°C) because that temperature corresponds to the right sugar concentration; a low-sugar jam will never reach it and does not need to. The set comes from calcium, not from boiling down.
Test on a frozen plate anyway. A spoonful should firm up within a minute and hold a shape when pushed. Low-sugar jams often look alarmingly loose in the pot and set properly in the jar overnight.
Fill hot jars to a quarter inch headspace, debubble, wipe the rims until they squeak, fit lids finger tight, and process for the tested time you looked up, timed from a full boil.
Cool overnight undisturbed and check the seals. Any jar that did not seal goes in the fridge.

If you would rather not can at all, this recipe is a perfectly good refrigerator jam. Skip the processing entirely, cool it, and keep the jars in the fridge for about three weeks, or in the freezer for a year.
notes: Regular pectin and low-methoxyl pectin are not interchangeable. Using regular pectin with half the sugar produces syrup, every time.
Do not reduce the sugar in a recipe written for regular pectin and expect it to be safe or to set. Use a recipe designed for the amount of sugar you actually want to use.
storage: Sealed and processed, a year in a cool cupboard, though the colour fades faster than a full-sugar jam. Once opened, about two to three weeks in the fridge rather than a month, because there is less sugar holding the water.

title: Freezer Jam
dek: No canner, no boiling, and it tastes more like the fruit than anything you cook.
intro:
Freezer jam is uncooked or barely cooked fruit set with pectin and stored cold. Because the fruit never boils, the colour stays bright and the flavour stays raw and immediate in a way that no cooked jam manages. It is the closest thing to eating the berry in the middle of winter.

To be completely clear about what this is: it is not canned and it is not shelf stable. It lives in the freezer, and once opened it lives in the fridge, and it is not safe to store at room temperature. That is a feature rather than a limitation, since it means no canner, no processing and no altitude tables.

items: 4 cups granulated sugar, or the amount your pectin specifies
1 packet powdered pectin labelled for freezer jam, or 3 tbsp instant pectin
3/4 cup water, if your pectin calls for it
6 freezer-safe jars or plastic containers with tight lids

method: Read your pectin package first. Freezer jam pectins differ: some are stirred straight into sugar and fruit cold, some need a brief boil with water. Follow the one you bought rather than a generic ratio.
Crush the berries with a potato masher rather than blending them. A blender aerates the jam and turns it pink and foamy, and it pulverises the seeds.
Stir the sugar into the crushed fruit and let it stand 10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the sugar has completely dissolved and the mixture looks glossy instead of grainy.

If your pectin needs cooking, bring it to a boil with the water and boil for one minute exactly, stirring, then pour it into the fruit. Boiling longer breaks the pectin down and it will not set at all.
Stir the fruit and pectin together for three full minutes by the clock. This is the step people cut short and it is what distributes the pectin. Under-stirred freezer jam sets in patches.
Add the bottled lemon juice and stir it through. It brightens the flavour and helps the set.
Ladle into containers, leaving a good half inch of headspace, because the jam expands as it freezes and a full jar will push its lid off or crack.

There is no gel stage here and no internal temperature to hit. A cooked jam is judged at 220°F (105°C) on a thermometer; this one sets chemically at room temperature and a thermometer tells you nothing useful about it.
Leave the containers on the counter, lids on, for 24 hours to set. It will look far too loose at the start; freezer pectin takes most of a day to firm up and there is no way to hurry it.
Label every container and move them to the freezer, keeping one in the fridge to start on.
If it has not set after a day, it will not. Use it as a syrup on pancakes or ice cream, which is a perfectly good outcome, or reprocess it with a fresh batch of pectin per the package instructions.
notes: This is a refrigerator and freezer preserve. It has not been processed, it is not shelf stable, and it must not be stored in a cupboard.
Any fruit works, but very low-acid fruit sets poorly. Berries, stone fruit and rhubarb are all reliable.
storage: In the freezer, up to a year with good colour and flavour. In the fridge, about three weeks once thawed or opened. Never at room temperature.

title: Apple Butter
dek: Hours of nothing happening, then suddenly it is dark and thick and smells like the whole house.
intro:
Apple butter is apple sauce cooked until the sugars caramelise and the water is gone, which takes far longer than seems reasonable and cannot be rushed with higher heat without scorching. There is no butter in it. The name refers to the texture, which should be spreadable and completely smooth with no grain at all.

Apples are high-acid fruit, so a boiling water bath is the correct process. Low-acid foods, meaning plain vegetables, meats, fish and soups, are never water bath safe and require a pressure canner. Fruit butters sit safely on the right side of that line, which is why this one can be canned at all.

items: 6 lb (2.7 kg) apples, cored and chopped, peels on
1 heavy pot or a slow cooker
1 food mill or an immersion blender
1 boiling water canner with a rack
1 copy of the current USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning, or OSU Extension

method: Get the tested processing time before you begin, from the USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning or from OSU Extension. It depends on jar size and altitude, and this page does not print one.

Note the altitude question. Siletz is near sea level and the base figures apply here, but water boils cooler as you climb and the tested tables add time accordingly. Use the line for your own elevation, not somebody else's.
Use a mix of apples. Tart ones for flavour, sweet ones for body. Leave the peels on while cooking; they carry pectin and colour and they come out in the mill.
Cook the apples with the cider, covered, over medium-low heat until they have completely collapsed and a spoon meets no resistance at all, about 40 minutes.
Pass everything through a food mill to remove peel and any remaining core, or blend it smooth if you peeled the apples first. The texture should be completely without grain.
Return the puree to the pot with both sugars, lemon juice, spices and salt, and stir until the sugar has dissolved.

Now cook it down, uncovered, over the lowest heat that keeps it moving, stirring often and scraping the bottom. This takes four to six hours on a stove or overnight in a slow cooker with the lid propped. It will spit; a splatter screen is worth it.

It is done when the volume has roughly halved, the colour has gone from pale to a deep mahogany brown, and a spoonful mounded on a cold plate holds its shape with no ring of liquid seeping out around it. That ring test is the whole doneness cue and it is more reliable than any timing.

A thermometer is of limited use here. Fruit butter finishes below the 220°F (105°C) gel stage of a jam because it is thickened by evaporation rather than by sugar concentration, so the plate test is what you go by.
Taste and adjust the spice at the end. Flavours concentrate enormously during the long cook and a mixture that seemed well spiced at the start can be overwhelming by the finish.
Ladle boiling hot into hot jars, leaving a quarter inch of headspace, remove bubbles, wipe the rims until they squeak, and fit lids and rings finger tight.

Process in the boiling water canner for the tested time, with jars covered by at least an inch of water, timed from a full rolling boil. Rest, lift out, cool overnight, and check every seal the next day.

What goes wrong: scorching. Once apple butter catches on the bottom of the pot, the burnt flavour goes through the entire batch within minutes and cannot be stirred out. Low heat and a heavy pot are not suggestions.
notes: A slow cooker with the lid set slightly ajar is the low-effort version and it is genuinely good. It just takes all night.
Nobody here has cooked your batch. Use a tested process, and if a jar looks or smells wrong on opening, dispose of it without tasting.
storage: Sealed jars, rings removed, a year in a cool dark cupboard. Opened, refrigerate and use within about a month. Unprocessed apple butter is a fridge product only and keeps three weeks.

title: Pepper Jelly
dek: Sweet, hot, and acid enough for a water bath because of the vinegar, not in spite of it.
intro:
Pepper jelly is a jelly made from peppers, sugar, pectin and a serious quantity of vinegar, and that vinegar is not a flavouring decision. Peppers on their own are a low-acid vegetable and are not safe in a boiling water bath. The added vinegar is what pushes the finished product into the high-acid range where water bath processing works.

Which means the one thing you must never do is reduce the vinegar because the jelly tastes sharp. Adjust the sugar, adjust the peppers, adjust the heat, but leave the acid alone and use a tested recipe's ratio.

items: 2 cups finely chopped red and green bell peppers, seeds out
1/2 cup finely chopped jalapenos or hotter chiles, to taste
1.5 cups cider vinegar of at least 5 percent acidity
1 heavy wide pot, at least 6 quarts
6 half-pint jars with new lids and sound rings
1 boiling water canner with a rack
2 pairs of gloves for handling chiles
1 copy of the current USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning, or your OSU Extension office

method: Get the tested processing time before you start, from the USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning or from OSU Extension, for your jar size. It also varies by altitude, and this page prints no number.

Note your elevation. Siletz is near sea level so the base figures apply here, but water boils cooler higher up and the tested tables add time to compensate. Look yours up rather than borrowing somebody else's.

Understand the acid. Peppers are low-acid and would need a pressure canner on their own. The vinegar at the stated strength and quantity is what makes this water bath safe, so use vinegar labelled at 5 percent acidity and do not dilute or reduce it.
Wear gloves to chop the chiles and keep your hands away from your face. This is obvious advice that people ignore once each.
Chop the peppers very fine, by hand or with a few pulses in a food processor, stopping well short of a puree. You want visible flecks suspended in clear jelly.
Combine peppers, vinegar, sugar and salt in the pot and bring it to a boil over high heat, stirring until the sugar has completely dissolved and the liquid runs clear rather than cloudy off a spoon.
Boil hard for 5 minutes, stirring, then add the liquid pectin all at once and return it to a full rolling boil that cannot be stirred down. Boil exactly one minute and take it off the heat.

Skim the foam. At this point the jelly will be very loose and that is correct; liquid pectin sets as it cools rather than by boiling down, so do not keep cooking it hoping for a gel stage at 220°F (105°C) the way you would with jam.
Let the pot stand 5 minutes and stir once. This stops all the pepper floating to the top of every jar, which is the classic cosmetic failure of pepper jelly.
Ladle into hot jars leaving a quarter inch of headspace, debubble, wipe the rims until they squeak, and fit lids and rings finger tight.
Process in the boiling water canner for the tested time, jars covered by an inch of water, timed from the return to a full rolling boil. Rest 5 minutes, lift out, and leave them overnight.
Check every seal the next day and refrigerate anything that failed. The jelly firms fully over about two days, so do not panic on the first night.
What goes wrong: a jelly that stays syrupy. Usually the pectin was old, or it was boiled for longer than a minute after the pectin went in, which breaks it down.
notes: Never describe a home canning recipe as safe on the strength of one batch. Use tested recipes, and dispose of any jar that is bulging or smells wrong without tasting it.
Over cream cheese with crackers is the standard use, and it is standard because it works.
storage: Sealed jars, rings off, a year in a cool dark cupboard. Opened, refrigerate and use within about two months.

title: Quick Pickled Onions
dek: Ten minutes of work, an hour of waiting, and they go on everything for the next month.
intro:
Pink pickled onions are the single highest return per minute of anything in this collection. They cut through the fat in a taco, a crab melt, a venison sandwich and a bowl of chowder, and they take ten minutes of actual work. The colour comes from the onion reacting with the acid, and it happens on its own within the hour.

Be clear about what this is: a refrigerator pickle. It is not processed, it is not shelf stable, and it lives in the fridge. That is not a shortcut, it is a different category of preserve with its own honest shelf life.

items: 3 large red onions, sliced paper thin
2 cups boiling water for blanching, optional
1.5 cups white wine vinegar or cider vinegar at 5 percent acidity

method: Slice the onions as thinly as you can manage, ideally on a mandoline. Thick slices stay harsh and crunchy in the middle and never take the brine evenly.
If you want a milder result, pour boiling water over the sliced onions in a sieve and drain them immediately. This knocks the raw sulphurous edge off without cooking them.
Pack the onions into two clean pint jars along with the bay, peppercorns, coriander, garlic, chiles and oregano, pressing them down firmly.
Combine the vinegar, water, sugar and salt in a small pan and heat, stirring, until the sugar and salt have completely dissolved and the liquid is steaming but not yet at a rolling boil.

There is no internal temperature to chase here. The brine only has to be hot enough to dissolve the salt and sugar and to soften the onion slightly; it is the acid, not the heat, doing the preserving.
Pour the hot brine over the onions to cover them completely. Anything sticking above the liquid discolours and goes soft.
Press the onions down with a spoon to release trapped air, let the jars cool on the counter for about an hour, and watch the colour go from purple to bright pink.
Lid them and refrigerate. They are edible after an hour, good after four, and best after a day.

On canning these: it is possible to process pickled onions in a boiling water bath, because added vinegar puts them in the high-acid range. But do that only with a tested recipe, with its stated vinegar strength, brine ratio, jar size and processing time, from the USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning or OSU Extension. Do not water bath this refrigerator recipe on the assumption that it is close enough.
Altitude affects any water bath process, and the tested tables account for it. Siletz is near sea level; a great many readers are not, and the correct time is the one for your own elevation.
What goes wrong: a weak brine. Cutting the vinegar with more water because the smell is strong gives you a pickle that goes slimy in the fridge in a fortnight.
notes: This is a refrigerator pickle and it has not been processed. It is not shelf stable and it must not be stored in a cupboard.
The leftover brine is excellent in a vinaigrette, and it will pickle a second, smaller batch of onions before it gives up.
storage: In the fridge, sealed, about a month. They soften gradually after two weeks and are still perfectly good, just less crisp. Discard if the brine turns cloudy or ropey.

title: Refrigerator Pickles
dek: Crisp, sour, and never processed, which is stated here on purpose.
intro:
Refrigerator pickles skip the canner entirely, which means they skip the heat that turns a canned cucumber soft. They stay genuinely crisp, they take twenty minutes, and they are ready in two days. The trade is that they live in the fridge and they do not keep for a year.

This is worth saying plainly because the difference between a refrigerator pickle and a canned one is a safety difference, not a convenience one. An unprocessed jar has not been heated enough to be shelf stable no matter how much vinegar is in it, and it belongs in the cold.

items: 3 lb (1.4 kg) small pickling cucumbers, blossom ends trimmed off
3 tbsp pickling or kosher salt for the pre-salt
3 cups vinegar at 5 percent acidity, white or cider
2 heads fresh dill, or 1 tbsp dill seed
1 grape leaf or 1/4 tsp black tea leaves, for crispness

method: Trim the blossom end off every cucumber, taking a good sixteenth of an inch. That end carries an enzyme that softens pickles, and it is the most common reason a jar goes limp.
Layer the cucumbers with the salt and ice in a bowl and leave them 2 hours. This draws water out and firms them up, which is the second half of the crispness question.
Rinse them well and dry them. Skipping the rinse leaves them far too salty once the brine goes in as well.
Pack the cucumbers upright into clean quart jars, tightly, with the aromatics tucked in around them. Add the grape leaf or the tea, which contribute tannins that help keep them firm.
Heat the vinegar, water, sugar and salt together, stirring, until everything is fully dissolved and the brine is steaming and clear. It does not need to boil hard.
No internal temperature applies to a refrigerator pickle. The brine is heated only to dissolve the salt and sugar, which is exactly why these stay crisp and exactly why they are not shelf stable.
Pour the hot brine over to cover the cucumbers completely, leaving about half an inch of space at the top. Anything above the liquid line will spoil first.
Tap the jars on the counter to release air bubbles, lid them, and let them cool on the counter before refrigerating.
Wait 48 hours before opening. They are edible sooner and they taste raw and disjointed; the brine needs two days to get to the middle of a whole cucumber.

If you want shelf-stable pickles instead, that is a different project. Use a tested recipe with a stated brine ratio and processing time from the USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning or OSU Extension, and expect a softer pickle as the price of the process. Do not simply water bath this recipe.

Processing time for any canned pickle depends on jar size and on altitude. Siletz is close to sea level, so base figures apply here; readers higher up need the line in the tested table that matches their own elevation.
What goes wrong: soft pickles. Blossom end left on, cucumbers too large, brine too weak, or a jar that sat warm too long before it went in the fridge. In that order of likelihood.
notes: These are refrigerator pickles. They have not been processed, they are not shelf stable, and they are not safe stored at room temperature.
Sliced spears take the brine much faster than whole cucumbers and are ready overnight. They also go soft sooner.
storage: In the fridge, about two months, staying crisp for the first three or four weeks. Throw out any jar with cloudy or ropey brine, a bad smell, or mould of any kind.

title: Canned Pears in Light Syrup
dek: High-acid fruit, a boiling water bath, and a processing time you go and look up.
yield: About 7 quart jars from a half bushel
intro:
Pears are the one fruit worth canning even if you never can anything else, because a good canned pear is closer to a fresh ripe one than any other preserved fruit gets. They are also high-acid, which is why a boiling water bath is the right and safe process for them. Low-acid foods, meaning plain vegetables, meats, fish and soups, are never water bath safe and require a pressure canner.

The trick with pears is ripeness. They ripen off the tree, from the inside out, and a pear canned rock hard stays woody in the jar forever. Let them come to the point where the flesh at the neck gives to a thumb.

items: 20 lb (9 kg) firm-ripe pears, Bartlett or similar
1 gallon water with 3 tbsp bottled lemon juice, as a holding solution
1 tsp ascorbic acid powder, optional, for colour
7 quart jars with new lids and sound rings
1 boiling water canner with a rack, deep enough to cover quarts by an inch
1 jar lifter, 1 wide funnel, 1 bubble tool
1 copy of the current USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning, or OSU Extension

method: Look up the tested processing time for pears in your jar size, hot packed, in the USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning or with OSU Extension. Quarts and pints differ, and altitude changes it again. This page does not print a number for you to apply to the wrong jar.

Find your altitude and use the line that matches. Siletz is near sea level, so the sea level figures apply here. Anyone inland or up a hill needs more time, and the tested table says exactly how much.
Ripen the pears at room temperature until the flesh just below the stem yields to gentle thumb pressure. Underripe pears go woody and stay that way; overripe ones fall apart into the syrup.
Peel, halve and core them with a melon baller, and drop each half straight into the lemon water. Cut pear browns within a minute of meeting air.

Make the syrup by heating the water and sugar together until fully dissolved and clear, then keep it hot. A light syrup lets the pear taste like a pear; heavier syrups hold shape and colour slightly better and taste like dessert.

Hot pack the fruit, which is what the tested times above assume. Simmer the drained pear halves in the syrup for 5 minutes, until they are heated through and look translucent at the edges but still hold their shape on a spoon.

Hot packing matters. Fruit going into the jar already hot drives out air and shortens the time the centre of the jar needs to reach process temperature. You are not probing for an internal temperature here; the tested process time is what does the work.
Pack the hot halves into hot jars, cavity side down and overlapping like roof tiles, and ladle hot syrup over to leave half an inch of headspace.
Run the bubble tool down the inside of each jar and adjust the syrup level after the air comes out. Wipe every rim until it squeaks and fit lids and rings finger tight.
Lower the jars onto the rack in the canner with water already hot, add water to cover them by at least an inch, and bring it to a full rolling boil.

Start timing only when it is at a full boil, and process for the tested time you looked up. Keep the water boiling the entire time; if it drops off the boil, bring it back and start the timing again from the beginning.
Turn off the heat, wait 5 minutes with the lid off, then lift jars straight up onto a towel with space between them and leave them undisturbed overnight.
Check the seals the next day. A sealed lid is concave and does not move when pressed. Refrigerate anything unsealed and eat it within a few days.
Never taste from a jar that is bulging, that spurts when opened, that smells fermented, or whose contents look wrong. Dispose of it following the instructions in the USDA guide.
notes: Nobody at this store has canned your particular batch. Follow tested processes from a current source, because home canning is the one place in cooking where improvising has consequences you cannot taste coming.
Very ripe pears are better made into pear butter or sauce than canned as halves. They will not hold their shape.
storage: Sealed jars with the rings removed keep well over a year in a cool dark cupboard, with best quality in the first year. Once opened, refrigerate and use within about a week.

title: Berry Syrup
dek: For pancakes, soda water and the bottom of a glass of something stronger.
intro:
Syrup is the useful thing to make from berries that are too soft for pie and too far gone for jam. It is fruit juice and sugar cooked briefly, which means the flavour stays bright rather than going jammy, and it is the only preserve on this list that improves a glass of soda water.

Written here as a refrigerator and freezer preserve, deliberately. Tested water bath processes for fruit syrups do exist and they work, but they belong to a tested recipe with its own ratios and times, not to this one.

items: 10 cups berries, about 1.4 kg, any combination
3 cups granulated sugar, adjusted to taste
1 vanilla bean or 1 tsp vanilla extract, optional
1 jelly bag or 4 layers of cheesecloth in a sieve
4 clean bottles or jars with tight lids

method: Put the berries and water in a wide pot and heat gently, crushing with a masher as they go, until the fruit has completely collapsed and the juice runs freely, about 10 minutes. Do not boil it hard; hard boiling extracts bitterness from seeds.
Add the first measure of lemon juice, take it off the heat, and let it stand 10 minutes.
Pour everything into a jelly bag or a cheesecloth-lined sieve set over a bowl and let it drip for at least 2 hours, or overnight in the fridge.
Do not squeeze the bag. Squeezing forces fine pulp through and gives you a cloudy syrup. If you want cloudy syrup with more body, squeeze on purpose and own the decision.
Measure the juice you got and combine it with the sugar in a clean pot, in roughly a four to three ratio by volume, along with the second lemon measure and the salt.
Heat gently, stirring, until every grain of sugar has dissolved and the liquid runs clear off a spoon rather than looking grainy.

Bring it to a gentle boil and cook 5 minutes, until it has thickened just enough to coat the back of a spoon and leave a brief track when you drag a finger through it. It should stay pourable; syrup thickens noticeably as it cools.
Do not take this to the jam gel stage. A thermometer reading 220°F (105°C) means you have made jelly, not syrup, and there is no way back short of adding water and starting over.
Skim any foam, add the vanilla off the heat, and pour into clean bottles while hot, leaving headspace if any are going to the freezer.
Cool, lid, and refrigerate. This is a refrigerator preserve; it has not been processed and it is not shelf stable, so it does not belong in a cupboard.

If you want shelf-stable syrup, use a tested water bath recipe from the USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning or from OSU Extension, with its stated ratios, jar size and processing time. Times change with altitude, and while Siletz is near sea level, plenty of readers are not.
notes: The drained pulp is not waste. Push it through a food mill and it becomes a rough fruit butter, or spread it thin and dry it into fruit leather.
Marionberry, blackberry, raspberry and huckleberry all work. Blue-toned berries make the best colour and strawberry makes the worst.
storage: Refrigerated in a sealed bottle, about a month. Frozen in containers with headspace, a year. It has not been canned and it is not safe at room temperature.

title: Shortcake
dek: A biscuit, not a sponge, and the berries need half an hour to make their own syrup.
intro:
Shortcake in this country is a sweetened biscuit split and filled, not the yellow sponge cups sold in plastic trays. The difference matters, because a biscuit has structure and salt and butter and can stand up to a pile of wet fruit, and a sponge cup dissolves into pink mush within four minutes.

The other half of the recipe is macerating. Sugar on cut berries pulls out juice by osmosis and makes a syrup that is better than anything you could cook, and it takes half an hour of doing nothing. That syrup is really the point of the dish.

items: 8 cups strawberries or mixed berries, hulled and sliced

method: Toss the berries with sugar, lemon and salt and leave them at room temperature at least 30 minutes, stirring once or twice, until a pool of dark syrup has collected in the bottom of the bowl.
Heat the oven to 425°F (220°C) and line a sheet pan with parchment.
Whisk the flour, sugar, baking powder, soda and salt. Cut in the cold butter with your fingertips until the largest pieces are pea-sized and the rest is coarse.
Pour in the buttermilk and stir with a fork until it just comes together, with dry patches still showing. Stop early. A shortcake dough that looks finished in the bowl is overmixed.
Tip it onto the counter, pat it into a rectangle, and fold it in thirds like a letter. Do that twice more. Those folds are what make the biscuit pull apart in layers instead of crumbling.
Pat to about an inch thick and cut eight rounds with a sharp cutter, pressing straight down without twisting. Twisting seals the edges and the biscuit cannot rise there.
Brush the tops with cream, scatter coarse sugar, and chill the tray for 10 minutes.

Bake until the biscuits have risen tall, the tops are deep golden, and the sides look dry and set rather than damp. A skewer into the middle of one should come out clean, and if you want the number, an instant-read thermometer in the centre reads about 200°F (93°C) when a biscuit is baked through.
Cool on a rack 10 minutes. Split them with your fingers rather than a knife, which follows the natural layer and gives you two rough faces that hold syrup.
Whip the cream with the powdered sugar and vanilla to soft peaks that just hold their shape and flop over at the tip. Stiff whipped cream is grainy and it slides off.
Build: bottom half, cream, berries with plenty of syrup, top half at an angle, more berries. Assemble at the table, because a built shortcake starts collapsing immediately.
What goes wrong: warm butter and heavy hands. Both give you a dense scone rather than a light biscuit, and the fruit will drown it.
notes: Local honey whipped into the cream instead of powdered sugar is very good and slightly less sweet.
The biscuits freeze unbaked on a tray and bake from frozen, adding a few minutes. That makes this a fifteen minute dessert in season.
storage: Biscuits are best the day they are made and acceptable the next, refreshed in a hot oven for a few minutes. Macerated berries keep two days in the fridge and get better on the first one.

title: The Gel Stage, and How to Test For It
dek: Jam does not set because it never got there. That is nearly always the answer.
yield: One reliable test you can trust
intro:
A jam sets because three things line up: pectin, acid and sugar concentration. The first two you supply at the start, and the third only arrives once enough water has boiled away. The gel stage is simply the moment the sugar concentration is high enough for the pectin to build a network, and it happens at a specific temperature because boiling point rises as syrup concentrates.

So when jam does not set, the usual reason is not bad pectin or bad luck. It is that the pot came off the heat too early. Here are three tests, and the reasons to use more than one.

items: 1 candy or jam thermometer that you have checked in boiling water
1 pot of jam at a full rolling boil
1 timer for the intervals between tests

method: Calibrate first. Put your thermometer in plain boiling water and read it. At sea level, which includes Siletz, water boils at 212 degrees Fahrenheit (100°C), and the gel stage sits about 8°C above that, which is 220°F (105°C).

Adjust for altitude by measuring, not by arithmetic. Whatever your water boiled at, the gel stage is roughly 8°C above that number. This is why a fixed target temperature copied from a recipe fails for people up a hill.

Test one, the thermometer. Keep the bulb in the jam and off the bottom of the pot. It is the fastest test and it is only as good as your calibration and your patience, since jam sits near the target for a while before crossing it.

Test two, the frozen plate, which is the one to trust. Take the pot off the heat, put a small spoonful on a plate from the freezer, and wait 30 seconds. Push it with a fingertip. Set jam wrinkles ahead of your finger and holds the track. Unset jam floods back into the gap.
Take the pot off the heat while you test. Thirty seconds of hard boiling while you are looking at a plate is enough to overshoot, and overshot jam is stiff and dull.

Test three, the sheet test. Dip a cold metal spoon and hold it sideways over the pot. Loose syrup runs off in drops. Jam approaching the gel stage runs off in two streams that merge and fall together as a sheet off the edge of the spoon.
Use at least two of the three. The thermometer tells you when to start testing; the plate tells you when to stop cooking.

Know what else affects it. Underripe fruit has more pectin than ripe fruit. Too little acid and the network cannot form, which is why lemon juice is in nearly every jam recipe. Too much sugar and it sets hard and candied; too little and it may never set at all without a low-sugar pectin.

Understand that added pectin changes the rules. Liquid and powdered pectins set on a timed boil rather than at a temperature, and pushing them to 220°F (105°C) breaks them down and guarantees the opposite of what you want. Follow the packet.

If it did not set, you can fix it. Pour it back into a pot, bring it to a rolling boil, and cook it to the gel stage properly. If you are canning it, that means clean jars, new lids and processing again for the tested time from a current source such as the USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning or OSU Extension.
And if it still will not set, stop. Call it syrup, put it on pancakes and ice cream, and move on. Every person who preserves has a shelf of jars quietly relabelled in their head.
notes: Jam continues to firm for up to two days in the jar. Do not judge a batch on the first night and re-boil something that would have been fine.
A digital probe thermometer is more accurate than a clip-on candy thermometer and far easier to keep off the bottom of the pot.
storage: Keep the frozen plates in the freezer permanently through berry season. It is the cheapest piece of equipment in the kitchen and the one that saves the most batches.
